title: Coq au Vin
subtitle: French chicken braised in red wine
excerpt: Coq au vin is a French farmhouse braise of chicken legs cooked slowly in red wine with lardons, mushrooms and herbs. It is forgiving, reheats beautifully, and tastes better the day after it is made.
sourceNotes: Coq au vin is a rustic French braise originally made with an old cockerel, whose tough meat benefited from long cooking in wine. Modern versions use chicken legs and a shorter braise time.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions for up to 3 months.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Coq au vin improves overnight. Make it a day ahead and reheat gently before serving.

content.text: Coq au vin is built in layers: the lardons go in first to render their fat, the chicken legs are browned in that fat, and then the whole lot braises together in wine with vegetables and herbs. Chicken legs are the right cut here because they stay moist and tender during the long braise; breasts would dry out.

Red wine is essential to the classic recipe: pour in a full bottle (750ml) of red wine and reduce the stock to 100ml. If cooking without alcohol, use all chicken stock and add a tablespoon of red wine vinegar for acidity.
The mushrooms are added for the last 20 minutes so they keep their texture rather than collapsing into the sauce. Serve with mashed potato, buttered noodles, or crusty bread.

Pat the chicken legs dry with kitchen paper and season all over with salt and pepper. Set the large saucepan over a medium heat. Add the lardons without any oil and cook for 5 to 6 minutes until the fat has rendered and the lardons are golden. Remove with a slotted spoon and set aside.

Increase the heat to medium-high and add the sunflower oil to the pan. Brown the chicken legs skin-side down for 5 to 6 minutes until the skin is deep golden and releases easily from the pan. Turn and brown the other side for 3 minutes. Remove and set aside.
Reduce the heat to medium. Add the butter, then the onion and carrot. Cook for 6 to 8 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and tomato puree and cook for 2 minutes more.

Scatter the flour over the vegetables and stir to coat. Cook for 1 minute, then gradually pour in the wine (or stock if not using wine), scraping up the browned bits from the base of the pan. Add the remaining stock, thyme and bay leaves. Return the chicken legs and lardons to the pan.
Bring to a gentle simmer, then cover and cook over a low heat for 50 minutes, keeping the liquid at a bare simmer throughout.
Remove the lid and add the mushrooms. Stir gently and continue cooking uncovered for 20 to 25 minutes until the sauce has reduced to a glossy consistency and the chicken is completely tender.
Discard the bay leaves and thyme sprigs. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve directly from the pan.

items.symptom: The chicken skin is pale and soft
items.cause: The pan was not hot enough when the chicken went in, or the skin was wet.
items.fix: Pat the skin completely dry before browning. Give each leg a full 5 to 6 minutes without moving it before you try to turn it; the skin will release naturally when it is properly browned.

items.cause: The flour was not sufficient to thicken the large volume of wine, or the lid was on throughout.
items.fix: Once the chicken is cooked, remove it to a warm plate, then simmer the sauce uncovered on a higher heat for 10 to 15 minutes to reduce. Return the chicken to reheat briefly before serving.

items.cause: The braise ran too hot or too long.
items.fix: Chicken legs are fairly forgiving, but a fierce simmer will still dry them out. Keep the heat as low as possible while maintaining a gentle bubble. If serving the next day, reheat very gently to avoid overcooking further.

items.symptom: The sauce tastes raw and alcoholic
items.cause: The wine was not cooked off properly before the stock was added.
items.fix: After adding the wine and before covering the pan, allow it to bubble vigorously for a few minutes to cook off the raw alcohol. The smell will shift from sharp to mellow.
